blocks.text: It is proved that שחף sachaph is the gull or the cepphus, whence κεπφωθεὶς [kepphōtheis] Prov. VII, 22.

As the ostrich is a huge bird, so it has detained us long. Now in what follows we shall settle matters more briefly. And first presents itself שחף sachaph, entirely omitted by the Syrian; rendered by the Chaldeans שחפא sachpha; by the Arabs سَاف [sāf] saph; by the Samaritan ࠔࠅࠐࠀ sopha: words equally unknown. So no help comes from here. The Greeks, Jerome, Munster and Castalio explain it as the gull; Junius as the aesalon [merlin], as if on the authority of R. Judah; Diodati as la folica, that is, the fulica [coot], in the Italian version, but the same man in the French as la movette, that is, the gull; the Genevans and the English as the cuckoo; Arias as the phthisic bird, as if the name were taken from phthisis. For most of the Hebrews observe that this bird's name שחף sachaph alludes to שחפת sachepheth, a kind of disease, Levit. XXVI, 16. and Deut. XXVIII, 22, whether because the bird itself is subject to this disease, or because it produces it in those who eat its flesh. But it is not well enough known either what kind of disease שחפת sachepheth is. R. Selomo defines it: חולי שמשחפת את הבשר אנפו״ליש בלע״ז דומה לנפוח שהוקלה כפיחהו ומראית פניו זעיפה, a disease that inflates the flesh; in French you would call them blisters; one who suffers from it is like a man who puffs his cheek slightly, and has the look of an angry man. And David de Pomis: הוא חולי אשר יוליד אבעבועות כמו תפוחים לפי רש״י, It is a disease producing pustules like apples, as R. Selomo Jarchi says. Yet R. Selomo says nothing about apples. But instead of דומה לנפוח, Pomarius seems to have read in R. Selomo דומה לתפוח, like an apple: a reading which what follows plainly refutes. However that may be, R. Jonah defines this same disease very differently, as these words of Kimchi in his Lexicon show: פירשו רבי יונה בל׳שון ערבי סחא״ף והוא החולי שהגוף מתנונה בו, R. Jonah explains it as the disease called in Arabic sochaph, through which the body becomes מתנונה mathnuna, that is, מתחלשת ומתכחשת ומתדלדלת, weakened, and emaciated, and wasted. For so the word מתנונה mathnuna is rendered in the Aruch, taken from the Talmudic tractate Sota, ch. 4, fol. 26 a.
